newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria protesters keep up pressure on Socialists.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria protesters keep up pressure on Socialists.

text.p: Anti-government protesters kept up nationwide strikes and blockades around Bulgaria on Tuesday, the 30th consecutive day of demonstrations to demand a general election.
Angry students and opposition supporters stayed out all night to keep up barricades in sub-zero temperatures after the ruling Socialists defiantly unveiled a new cabinet containing many old faces.
Public transport did not run in Sofia for a second day and students kept up a blockade of the Eagles Bridge intersection overnight, lighting fires to keep warm.

Protesters from Doupnitsa, where townspeople have blocked road and rail routes to Greece since Wednesday, said they were heading for Sofia to set up their barricades outside parliament, which is due to vote on the new cabinet on Wednesday.
Prime minister-designate Nikolai Dobrev is due to present the cabinet to President Petar Stoyanov later in the day.
Opposition leader Ivan Kostov told Reuters main roads and railways were blocked around the country and the atmosphere was noticeably more tense.
"We have appealed to police and protesters to avoid any violence because we are all part of the suffering Bulgarian nation," he said.
Sofia shoppers queued for bread as flour supplies ran low. Petrol stations are also suffering shortages as the Neftohim refinery is running low on crude.
Standart daily came out with "Strike" printed in opposition blue across every page.
Miners at Maritsa East, Pernik and Bobov Dol are on indefinite strike, and Varna port is closed since Monday.
Air traffic controllers planned a one-hour stoppage from 3 p.m. until 4 p.m. (1300 GMT to 1400 GMT). On Monday, planes were allowed to land during a similar stoppage.
In Plovdiv, where the protests began on January 6, protesters kept up blockades overnight.
Sultana Raikova, secretary of the UDF protest comittee, said major roads out of town were blocked in both directions and the railway was closed.
"We are ready to step up our protests if any decision on a second Socialist government is taken," she said.
"This protest has been going on for quite a long time now. I hope we can soon re-form our protest committee into a pre-election committee."
The anti-government campaign has built into one of the biggest protests since the end of communist rule in 1989.

The Socialists were elected in December 1994 for a four-year term, but lost presidential elections in November. Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned in December after months of criticism of his handling of the economy, which has plunged far deeper into crisis since then.
A week after the lev hit 1,000 to the dollar on the interbank market for the first time, it was trading at 2,650 to 2,800 on Tuesday morning.
Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate with international lenders, draw up a 1997 budget and set up a tough fixed exchange rate regime to halt the slide of the lev.
Inflation was estimated at 50 percent last month and the central bank met its January payment on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt but is fast running out of foreign exchange.
